title: Artificially Intelligent Lawyers: Updating the Model Rules of Professional Conduct in Accordance with the New Technological Era
pub: Cardozo Law Review, vol. 39, no. 4, pp. 1497-1530 (2018)
author: Katherine Medianik

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The Note accepts the cluster’s core view that human oversight must involve independent professional judgment and evidence-checking, not nominal accountability. It materially develops that proposition by defining verification as independent legal research and proposing explicit amendments that would bring AI tools within lawyers’ supervision duties under the Model Rules.
qs: By checking I mean for attorneys to conduct their own independent legal research after ROSS presents its results in order to check whether ROSS’s results are on point and did not miss any important cases and/or statutes.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Medianik accepts the cluster’s supervised-aid model: lawyers retain responsibility, must exercise independent judgment, and must substantively check AI-assisted research. She materially extends it by proposing targeted Model Rule amendments and mandatory legal-technology education, while maintaining proportionate supervision that preserves delegation’s economic benefits.
qs: 20 Specifically, this Note proposes: (1) the addition of continuing legal education (CLE) requirements on “Legal Technology”; (2) the addition of the term “nonlawyer assistant” to the terminology section of the Model Rules; and (3) the addition of several comments that incorporate AI technology and account for technological advancement.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Medianik accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model: AI assists with research, while lawyers retain independent judgment, verification and responsibility. She materially extends it with concrete preventive governance proposals—AI-specific Model Rule guidance, technology CLE, and supervision and review obligations directed at lawyers using AI.
qs: Adding new terms and comments would place AI technology within the scope of Model Rules 1.1, 2.1, and 5.3, thereby providing lawyers with concrete instructions on how to stay competent, use independent professional judgment, and properly review the work that AI machines produce.

Further, law firms employing ROSS will need to have some verification process in place that determines whether ROSS’s search results are in fact accurate and support the arguments that the human lawyer is trying to make.

kp.k: Regulate lawyers using AI rather than AI itself
kp.d: Medianik's central recommendation is an evolutionist approach to professional ethics: mandatory legal-technology education, an express definition encompassing AI as nonlawyer assistance, and additional Model Rule comments. This is a preventive reform proposal, not a report of enacted AI-specific requirements.
qs: This Note does not propose to regulate AI technology itself, but rather to regulate the lawyers that use it.
Given the inevitable technological prevalence, the ABA needs to take action to revise the Model Rules in conformity with the new era.

kp.k: ROSS augments lawyers rather than independently practising law
kp.d: The article describes ROSS as a natural-language research tool that identifies authorities, monitors legal developments and assists with memoranda. Its account draws on vendor material and interviews, including a September 2016 interview with von Briesen & Roper CIO William Caraher. Caraher distinguishes this research platform from an autonomous attorney: licensed lawyers must frame questions and interpret results.
qs: In today’s reality, ROSS merely assists and supplements human intelligence by allowing human lawyers to be more efficient at what they do.
ROSS is not an autonomous system and doesn’t have a license to practice law in any state.
The current ROSS roadmap requires human intervention to ask the questions and interpret the results.

kp.k: Research efficiency changes costs and competitive positioning
kp.d: Medianik predicts that reduced research labour will enable lower prices, greater attention to complex advisory work and stronger firm margins. She cites ROSS-reported figures of 30.3% time savings over Boolean searches, 22.3% over natural-language searches and a $13,067 annual revenue increase per attorney; the article does not supply their sample or methodology. Caraher reports fewer billable research hours, while expected market-wide advantages remain the author's argument rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Second, it permits them to spend more time and money on high-value advisory tasks and complex legal matters.
ROSS has saved research time, which translates into fewer billable hours.
$13,067 annual revenue increase per attorney.

kp.k: Hiring benefits coexist with predicted labour displacement
kp.d: The article reports competing perspectives rather than establishing a net employment effect. Critics predict that automation of mundane work will reduce the lawyers needed to deliver services. In contrast, Caraher reports that ROSS had not negatively affected hiring at his firm and had attracted associates and lateral lawyers. Medianik also predicts client attraction through technological differentiation.
qs: ROSS hasn’t impacted in a negative way, in fact we have seen laterals and associates gravitate towards our firm because we are using such cutting-edge technology.
With this mindset, not only will the use of cutting-edge AI technology lure lawyers to firms, it will lure clients in as well.

kp.k: Automation spans discovery, forms, research and predictive analytics
kp.d: Drawing on McGinnis and Pearce and examples of existing products, the article describes automation extending beyond research to discovery, document creation and case-outcome analytics. It cites a reported reduction in incorporation-document work from about 20 to 40 billable hours to a handful. Future brief drafting and increasingly autonomous issue identification are attributed predictions; Caraher explicitly states that ROSS did not, to his knowledge, predict litigation success.
qs: Kira Systems can automatically highlight and extract important contract provisions and helps organize data for analysis
No, to my knowledge ROSS does not have a probability engine for the success of winning or losing a legal argument.
In the second phase, the AI machine will itself identify the issues and suggest case law that is relevant.

kp.k: Lower-cost forms could address unmet legal needs
kp.d: Medianik cites McGinnis and Pearce's argument that machine-assisted form generation could make services more affordable to low- and middle-income people with unmet needs, including small-business advice and prenuptial agreements. This is a proposed access-to-justice mechanism, not evidence that ROSS or other tools had measurably closed the justice gap.
qs: Lawyers can use machines to help generate relevant forms, thereby reducing the costs of providing services and making the services more broadly affordable.
These legal needs include matters as varied as counseling on small-business matters and writing prenuptial agreements.

kp.k: Technological competence requires practical skills beyond general awareness
kp.d: Medianik argues that Model Rule 1.1 Comment 8 acknowledges technological benefits and risks but provides insufficient operational guidance. Competent AI use requires correct question framing, recognition of relevant issues and jurisdictions, and interpretation of results. She distinguishes existing state approaches to technological competence from her proposed AI-specific education requirements.
qs: Comment 8 requires lawyers to be competent with the technology that they use, but does not tell lawyers how to do so to escape disciplinary action or sanctions.
For example, if an AI tool performs legal research, was it asked the right questions? Did it grasp the legal issue? Did it research the pertinent jurisdiction?

kp.k: Independent judgment requires verification and contextual client advice
kp.d: Under her interpretation of Model Rule 2.1, Medianik argues that blindly adopting AI research displaces the lawyer's independent professional judgment. Lawyers must verify applicability and accuracy and integrate clients' objectives, risk tolerance and relevant nonlegal considerations. Her proposed comment would require cross-checking AI results against traditional platforms before acting or advising, keeping AI in an assisting rather than autonomous role.
qs: In exercising independent professional judgment, lawyers must confirm
AI technology shall be used as an assisting tool to the human lawyer, not as an autonomous agent.

Since ROSS is nothing but a machine that produces results via coding patterns, ROSS is unable to make discretionary decisions and cannot simultaneously assess the nature, risks, and alternatives associated with the respective legal issues at hand.

kp.k: Growing trust can erode human verification
kp.d: Caraher's account supplies interview evidence that attorneys cross-checked ROSS less frequently as they found it accurate. Medianik treats this as a warning about complacency rather than proof of documented client harm. She argues that proprietary, opaque systems intensify the need for verification and that lawyers remain responsible despite confidence gained through satisfactory prior results.
qs: The more our attorneys used it and found that it was accurate, the less they felt they needed to cross check with the other platforms.
In other words, “the robot did it” cannot be an excuse when issues arise.

kp.k: AI supervision belongs within nonlawyer assistance rules
kp.d: Medianik reads the 2012 change in Rule 5.3's title from nonlawyer assistants to nonlawyer assistance as supporting application beyond humans. She proposes expressly defining nonlawyer assistants to include AI tools and requiring review before work reaches clients. Human-assistant disciplinary cases provide analogies for responsibility, not AI-specific holdings. Her proposed supervision standard preserves delegation's economic benefits by requiring reasonable rather than best efforts.
qs: Responsible supervision does not mean that the lawyer must duplicate the nonlawyer’s work or scrutinize and regulate it so closely that the economic and other advantages of the delegation are lost.
Paragraphs (a) and (b) require reasonable efforts, not best efforts.
Therefore, lawyer supervision may suffice with simple review that is not overly intricate or unduly burdensome.

kp.k: Mandatory technology education should precede client-facing use
kp.d: Medianik recommends specialty CLE credits in legal technology, potentially targeted to lawyers actually using particular tools, and suggests mandatory law-school technology courses or coverage within professional responsibility. She contrasts advance education with brief onboarding and trial-and-error learning described in firm and vendor accounts, arguing that training should occur before errors affect representation.
qs: Going even further, law schools can implement mandatory legal technology courses into their curricula or add the topic to the professional responsibility requirement.
For example, if law firms X, Y, and Z employ ROSS, only X, Y, and Z’s lawyers utilizing the technology ought to be required to take specialty credits in operating AI technology.
Either way, lawyers using AI should be trained to work with such technology before the stakes get too high.

kp.k: Certification proposals face opacity and continuous-development objections
kp.d: The article reports Matthew Scherer's proposed Artificial Intelligence Development Act as a federal certification and tort-liability framework, not enacted legislation. Medianik objects that regulators may lack system-specific expertise, evolving machine-learning systems complicate certification and recertification, and anticipated benefits might outweigh liability costs. These are arguments supporting lawyer-focused regulation, not empirical findings about regulatory performance.
qs: Therefore, this Note takes the position that the better option would be to regulate the attorney using the AI instead.
With that in mind, even if AIDA certifies the machine in its infancy stage, there is no way to know what it will become as it learns and develops.

kp.d: Medianik acknowledges the counterargument that AI-related incompetence and blind reliance have not been concretely established and that firms describe substantial human involvement. She nevertheless draws on earlier e-discovery failures, sanctions and education initiatives to argue for preventive action before analogous AI problems emerge. This is historical analogy and risk prediction, not evidence of AI-caused disciplinary incidents.
qs: It can be argued that there is no concrete evidence that lawyers are incompetent in using technology, nor that they are blindly relying on results that technological apparatuses provide.
Specifically, e-discovery was very controversial in its early stages because lawyers abdicated responsibility and blindly trusted the technology.
Similar issues are likely to arise with AI technology as well in the foreseeable future, and what better way to mitigate risk than to take preventive measures early on?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Medianik presents legal AI as an efficiency-enhancing assistant that changes research and routine work, creates competitive advantages, and increases the need for lawyer training, verification, and supervision.
pts.d: Medianik claims that ROSS accelerates research, monitors legal developments, and reduces research costs and billable hours, allowing lawyers to concentrate on higher-value advice and complex matters. She predicts that adopting firms can offer lower prices, achieve superior margins, attract clients and talented lawyers, and reinvest in growth, while non-adopters risk falling behind. She describes developing applications in document generation, contract analysis, and outcome prediction, drawing on cited scholarship and product examples rather than presenting original findings. Her account of current ROSS usage is augmentation, not autonomous replacement: licensed lawyers must ask questions, interpret results, and supply contextual judgment. Interviewee William Caraher reports positive recruitment effects rather than reduced associate hiring at his firm. Medianik nevertheless predicts that familiarity with apparently accurate AI results can erode verification. She argues that blind reliance can compromise competence, independent judgment, and supervision, exposing lawyers to discipline or malpractice claims. Her proposed response is mandatory technology education and amendments to the Model Rules' terminology and comments, regulating lawyers using AI rather than the technology itself.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of vendor statistics, interviews, adoption examples, cited scholarship, and legal analogies; the article does not report an independent empirical study of AI performance or professional misconduct.
pts.d: For research efficiency, Medianik reproduces ROSS's own statistics: 30.3% time savings over Boolean searches, 22.3% over natural-language searches, and a $13,067 annual revenue increase per attorney. These are vendor-reported figures; the article does not supply their study design. Her September 2016 email interview with Caraher supplies practitioner experience of reduced research time, favorable recruitment and client responses, and declining cross-checking as confidence grows. A telephone interview with ROSS co-founder Andrew Arruda supplies information about the system's functioning. Product examples and cited scholarship support the discussion of document automation and prediction. The competitive-market predictions extend these reported efficiencies through economic reasoning, rather than through measured market-wide changes. The proposed ethical safeguards rest on interpretations of Model Rules 1.1, 2.1, and 5.3, state ethics materials, and analogies to nonlawyer-supervision and e-discovery cases. Those cases are not instances of ROSS misconduct. Medianik acknowledges the counterargument that concrete evidence of technological incompetence or blind reliance is lacking, but argues for preventive action based on earlier e-discovery problems.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article distinguishes reported capabilities and experiences in its 2016–2018 context from near-future adoption predictions and longer-run risks as trust increases.
pts.d: Published in 2018, the article describes ROSS as an early-stage research tool already used by firms, with broader practice-area expansion anticipated. Its predictions of wider adoption, further automation, and competitive pressure generally use an unspecified near-future horizon rather than a dated forecast. Benefits depend on effective deployment by capable human lawyers; lower-price competition is discussed under a perfect-substitutes assumption. Caraher's September 2016 account expressly qualifies ROSS as nonautonomous and not an outcome-probability engine. Medianik's concern about diminished checking is conditional on lawyers becoming comfortable with the system and increasingly trusting its outputs. Her proposed Rule 2.1 comment requires cross-checking against traditional platforms before reliance, while her proposed Rule 5.3 comment qualifies supervision as reasonable rather than best efforts and says it should not eliminate delegation's economic benefits. Training is proposed before use in client representation, potentially restricted to lawyers actually using the relevant AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are adopting and non-adopting firms, practicing lawyers, clients, and professional regulators; the article also identifies potential benefits for people unable to afford legal help.
pts.d: Adopting law firms are expected to save research labor, redirect resources toward complex work, strengthen recruitment and marketing, and potentially gain pricing and margin advantages. Non-adopters face competitive disadvantage. Individual lawyers must learn to operate AI, frame appropriate questions, interpret answers, and verify work before advising clients; supervisors remain responsible for delegated work. Caraher's hiring observations concern his own firm and do not establish profession-wide employment effects. Clients may receive faster and cheaper services, but also bear risks from inaccurate or insufficiently contextualized advice if lawyers rely blindly on AI. The article separately cites the potential for automated forms and lower-cost delivery to address unmet legal needs among low- and middle-income people; this is a prospective access-to-justice benefit, not a measured outcome. The ABA, state bars, CLE providers, and law schools are asked to provide clearer standards and education. Proposed Model Rule changes are recommendations, not descriptions of enacted requirements.
